about: FormatMap ratings. Every number here is editable data: change a rating, add a format or tweak the scoring and the script picks it up. effort = production cost (1 = minutes on a phone, 10 = a small team for weeks). premium = how premium it feels to a viewer scrolling past (1 = obvious low effort, 10 = looks like a studio made it). hours = typical hours for one finished piece by a solo creator at that length. face = required | optional | none. platforms (optional) = where the format is native; a creator on none of them gets it left out. These are starting judgements, not measurements: adjust them per creator with 'overrides' in the scan file.

scale.effort: 1 = phone, one take, no edit; 3 = a light edit and captions; 5 = scripting, several shots, a real edit; 7 = animation or a shoot day; 10 = a team for weeks
scale.premium: 1 = reads as copy-paste; 3 = ordinary feed content; 5 = clearly made with care; 7 = looks like a media brand; 10 = looks like a studio production
scale.saturation: 0-10, how much of what this niche's audience is shown already uses the format. See references/niche-scan.md for the bands.

formats.name: Talking head
formats.definition: The creator speaks straight to camera, usually with captions and jump cuts.
examples: "3 mistakes I made in my first year of investing" filmed on a phone
A sit-down YouTube essay with one camera angle

polish: Light the face with one soft key light and a darker background, and grade for skin tone
Use a second angle or a punch-in crop every 6-10 seconds instead of constant jump cuts
insight: Open with a specific claim the viewer can't get from the first 5 search results
Back one point with something you did or measured yourself
novelty: Film somewhere that is part of the story (the workshop, the trading desk, the kitchen)
Cut to one proof shot (a screen, an object, a document) for every claim
detail: Write captions by hand: correct terms, emphasis on 1-2 words per line, no auto-caption errors
Match the cut points to sentence ends so it never feels chopped

formats.name: Green screen commentary
formats.definition: The creator talks over a screenshot, article, post or image behind them.
examples: Reacting to a headline with the article behind you
Explaining a chart someone else posted

polish: Recreate the screenshot as a clean, cropped, readable card instead of a blurry capture
Key out cleanly and add a soft shadow so you sit in the scene
insight: Add the one fact the original post left out
End with what the viewer should do differently, not only your opinion
novelty: Animate the background: highlight, zoom or annotate the exact line you're talking about
Swap backgrounds on each point so it moves like a slideshow
detail: Cite the source on screen with date
Blur names and handles of private people

formats.name: Text on B-roll
formats.definition: A short line of text over generic or stock footage, often with trending audio. The classic low-effort, copy-paste format.
examples: "Things nobody tells you about moving abroad" over a slow walking clip
A quote over a sunset clip

polish: Shoot your own footage that literally shows what the text says, not mood footage
Set the text in one consistent typeface, size and safe-area position
insight: Replace the generic line with a number, a named example or a counter-intuitive claim
Turn one line into a 3-beat mini argument across 3 shots
novelty: Make the text interact with the footage (behind objects, tracking, revealed by movement)
Use a recurring visual series hook the audience learns to recognise
detail: Time each line to be readable twice at normal speed
Pick audio that fits the claim, not just what's trending

formats.name: Carousel / slides
formats.definition: A swipeable set of images or slides (Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok photo mode).
examples: "7 budgeting rules" as 8 slides
A before/after case study across 5 slides

polish: Build a real grid and type system so every slide feels designed, not templated
Make slide 1 a strong visual, not a wall of text
insight: Give each slide one idea with a concrete example
Include one original diagram, table or framework the viewer will save
novelty: Make the swipe itself part of the story (a reveal, a zoom, a continuous image across slides)
Use real photos or screenshots instead of stock icons
detail: Check every slide at phone size for readability
Put the save-worthy summary on the last slide

formats.name: POV
formats.definition: A first-person scenario: "POV: you just..." acted or shown from the viewer's perspective.
examples: "POV: your first day as a junior developer"
Hands-only POV of opening a new product

polish: Shoot real first-person angles (head or chest mount) instead of a selfie
Use sound design so the scene feels physical
insight: Base the scenario on a real, specific situation the niche recognises
Hide one useful tip inside the scenario
novelty: Run a POV series with the same character and an ongoing story
Flip the perspective (POV of the customer, the boss, the object)
detail: Get the props and jargon exactly right for the niche
Keep it under the length the joke can carry

formats.name: Skit / sketch
formats.definition: A scripted scene with characters, often the creator playing several roles.
examples: "The client who wants it done yesterday" with the creator playing both sides
A recurring office-life sketch series

polish: Lock framing and continuity between characters; use real costumes or props
Mix dialogue properly so both voices sit at the same level
insight: Write from a real pain point so the punchline teaches something
Let the niche's insiders feel seen with one precise detail
novelty: Build recurring characters
Use an unexpected genre for a mundane niche topic
detail: Cut on the beat of the joke, not after it
Subtitle each character in a different colour

formats.name: Screen recording
formats.definition: A capture of the screen while the creator shows how to do something, usually with voiceover.
examples: "How to set up X in 60 seconds"
A full software walkthrough

polish: Record at high resolution with a clean desktop and hidden notifications
Add smooth zooms and cursor highlights to where the action is
insight: Show the result first, then how
Include the mistake most people make and how to avoid it
novelty: Rebuild the key screens as clean UI mockups instead of raw captures
Speed-ramp boring parts and keep the 'aha' moment in real time
detail: Blur personal data in every frame
Make on-screen text readable on a phone

formats.name: Hands-on tutorial
formats.definition: Step-by-step how-to filmed in the real world: cooking, crafts, fixing, fitness, makeup.
examples: A 45-second recipe
"How to replace a bike chain"

polish: Use two angles (overhead and close-up) and consistent lighting
Record clean sound of the process (chops, clicks, sizzles)
insight: Explain why each step matters, not only what to do
Show the failure version next to the right version
novelty: Add exact measurements and timing as clean on-screen graphics
Show the finished result in a real use moment
detail: Every step visible: no off-screen 'and then'
A pinned or on-screen summary of steps

formats.name: Listicle
formats.definition: A numbered list: "5 tools", "10 mistakes", "3 books".
examples: "5 apps I use every day"
"Top 10 budget travel destinations"

polish: Give each item its own visual (real shot, product, screenshot), never the same B-roll
Use a consistent numbered graphic system
insight: Rank them and justify the ranking
Cut the list to items you have actually used or tested
novelty: Add a twist item or a 'one I'd avoid'
Show a comparison table at the end
detail: Correct names, prices and dates on screen
Order by surprise, not alphabet

formats.name: Storytime
formats.definition: The creator tells a personal or true story, on camera or as voiceover.
examples: "How I lost my first client"
"The weirdest thing that happened at work"

polish: Cut to photos, documents or places from the story
Use a score that follows the tension
insight: End with the lesson in one sentence the viewer can reuse
Add the number or fact that makes it real
novelty: Reconstruct key moments with simple visuals (a map, a chat recreation, a timeline)
Tell it out of order with a hook from the ending
detail: Cut every sentence that doesn't move the story
Protect identities of other people in the story

formats.name: Faceless explainer (stock + voiceover)
formats.definition: Voiceover explaining a topic over stock footage, screenshots or AI images.
examples: "Why rent is so expensive" over city stock clips
A history channel with AI-generated stills

polish: Replace generic stock with visuals that literally show each sentence
Record or clone a voice with real pacing and warmth, and mix it with room tone and music
insight: Lead with a question the viewer actually has and answer it with one fresh source
Add one original chart or comparison
novelty: Give the channel a signature visual style (collage, glass UI, sketch) instead of stock
Use a recurring visual metaphor across episodes
detail: Fact-check every number and show the source
Remove watermarks and mismatched stock (wrong country, wrong era)

formats.name: Vox-style collage explainer
formats.definition: Mixed-media animated explainer: paper cut-outs, halftone photos, paint blocks, archival clippings, annotated with hand-drawn notes.
examples: "Why do airlines overbook?" with cut-out planes and newspaper clippings
A 10-minute history essay in paper collage

polish: Keep a tight palette (paper, black, one accent colour)
Animate on a stop-motion frame rate for the hand-made feel
insight: Anchor each segment on one primary source shown on screen
Script around one question, answered at the end
novelty: Pair it with a contrasting style for the answer (paper → glass)
Use real artefacts from the niche as collage material
detail: Credit archival material and check its licence
Make every clipping legible for at least one beat

formats.name: Motion graphics / kinetic type
formats.definition: Animated shapes, icons and typography carry the explanation, usually with voiceover.
examples: An animated "how compound interest works"
A kinetic-type quote video

polish: Use easing and one motion language everywhere
Design frames as stills first; animate second
insight: One idea per scene
Show the mechanism, not just the words
novelty: Let one shape carry through every transition
Mix in one real-world shot as contrast
detail: Sync key motions to voice emphasis
Check contrast and reading time

formats.name: Data visual / animated chart
formats.definition: A chart, map or number animates to tell a story: bar races, maps filling in, a line that drops.
examples: "How house prices changed since 1990" as an animated line
A map of where a product is banned

polish: One chart per point, clean labels, no gridline clutter
Animate the change, not the whole chart
insight: Show the one comparison that surprises people
Explain what the number means for the viewer's life
novelty: Use a real-world scale comparison
Combine the chart with a short human story
detail: Source and date on screen for every dataset
Start axes honestly

formats.name: Clean UI / product demo
formats.definition: Software or a solution shown as clean, Apple-like interface animation: glass panels, smooth cursor, close-ups of the UI in use.
examples: A 30-second app feature launch
"How this workflow saves 2 hours a week" with a rebuilt UI

polish: Rebuild the UI in vector instead of capturing pixels
Use one camera move per screen, with soft depth and shadow
insight: Show the before (messy) and after (clean) workflow
Put the time or money saved on screen
novelty: Make the UI react to the voiceover
Open on the problem in a contrasting style (paper → glass)
detail: Realistic data in the mock UI
Consistent cursor speed and click sounds

formats.name: Interview / street interview
formats.definition: Asking other people questions: passers-by, experts, customers.
examples: "What do you do for a living?" on the street
A 2-camera expert interview

polish: Lav mics on both people; two cameras
Consistent framing and grade across interviewees
insight: Ask one question that reveals something real (salary, mistakes, numbers)
Interview people the audience can't normally reach
novelty: A recurring question across cities or jobs
Add on-screen data that confirms or contradicts the answers
detail: Release forms
Caption names and roles correctly

formats.name: Podcast clip
formats.definition: A cut from a longer conversation, usually two speakers on mics.
examples: A 40-second hot take from an episode
A split-screen clip of two guests

polish: Reframe each speaker vertically with active-speaker switching
Clean the audio (de-noise, level both voices)
insight: Clip a complete idea with a beginning and a payoff, not a fragment
Add a one-line context card
novelty: Overlay B-roll or graphics for what's being described
Pair the clip with a stitch or follow-up answer
detail: Hand-checked captions
Name the guest on screen

formats.name: Mini-documentary
formats.definition: A researched, reported story with interviews, archive, field footage and narration.
examples: "The town that runs on one factory"
A 12-minute investigation of a product scam

polish: Plan a shot list; consistent grade and sound bed
Use archive and field footage, not only stock
insight: One original finding (a document, an interview, a number)
A clear question and an honest answer
novelty: Access nobody else has
A structure with a turn in the middle
detail: Fact-check and keep a source log
Licences for every archive clip

formats.name: Cinematic video essay
formats.definition: A narrated essay over intentionally shot footage, with a strong visual style.
examples: "Why I left the city" shot on a mirrorless camera with a score
An essay on a design trend with macro shots

polish: Shoot every shot for the line it covers
Score and grade as one mood
insight: A thesis in the first 20 seconds
A personal angle nobody else can claim
novelty: A visual motif that returns at the end
One unexpected location or technique
detail: Every cut motivated
Silence used on purpose

formats.name: Whiteboard / drawn explainer
formats.definition: The explanation is drawn by hand on paper, a tablet or a whiteboard while the voice explains.
examples: "How a credit score is calculated" drawn on an iPad
Sketch-note book summaries

polish: Overhead rig with no shadows; clean, consistent pen weights
Speed up the drawing to match speech
insight: Build one diagram that the viewer can screenshot
Draw the mental model, not the words
novelty: Combine drawings with real photos
A character who returns each episode
detail: Legible handwriting at phone size
Correct labels and units

formats.name: Case study breakdown
formats.definition: Taking a real example (a brand, an ad, a video, a company) apart and explaining why it worked or failed.
examples: "Why this ad got 10M views" with annotated frames
"How this shop doubled its sales"

polish: Annotate frames with clean arrows, circles and callouts
Show the original next to your annotation
insight: Name the principle and show it in a second example
Give the viewer a step to copy
novelty: Recreate the example yourself and show results
Compare winner vs. loser side by side
detail: Only quote numbers you can show the source for
Credit the original creator

formats.name: Before / after transformation
formats.definition: Shows a change: a room, a design, a body, a workflow, a website.
examples: A room makeover in 20 seconds
A logo redesign reveal

polish: Lock off the camera so before and after match exactly
Use a satisfying reveal transition
insight: Show the 2-3 decisions that made the difference
Give the cost or time it took
novelty: Let the viewer guess before the reveal
Show a fail version too
detail: Same lighting and angle both sides
Honest results, no hidden edits

formats.name: Process / satisfying (hands only)
formats.definition: Hands making or fixing something, with crisp natural sound and little or no talking.
examples: Restoring an old tool
Packing orders for a small shop

polish: Macro lens and close mic
Clean, consistent work surface and light
insight: One on-screen line explaining the technique
Show the reason behind a key step
novelty: An unusual material or object
A series with a counter (day 1, day 2...)
detail: No music over the best sounds
Loop the ending to the start

formats.name: Day in the life / vlog
formats.definition: Follows the creator (or a role) through a day.
examples: "Day in the life of a nurse"
A week of running a one-person business

polish: Plan 5-6 shots per scene instead of filming everything
Use natural sound and a consistent grade
insight: Add real numbers (hours, money, tasks)
One honest low point
novelty: A role the audience has never seen inside
A time-lapse or map motif
detail: Cut faster than you think
Protect other people's privacy

formats.name: Challenge / experiment
formats.definition: "I tried X for 30 days", tests, comparisons, side-by-side trials.
examples: "I tested 5 budget apps for a month"
"Which knife stays sharp longest?"

polish: Consistent test setup filmed the same way each time
A clear results graphic
insight: A fair method explained in one line
A result that surprised you
novelty: An experiment nobody in the niche has run
Let the audience vote on the next test
detail: Record the data as you go
Show the losing option fairly

formats.name: Review / comparison / buying advice
formats.definition: Judging products or options: a single review, a head-to-head, "best X under $Y", "don't buy this".
examples: "Is the cheapest espresso machine worth it?"
"Notion vs Obsidian after a year"

polish: Film every product the same way (same light, angle, background)
A clean verdict card per product
insight: Test on a criterion that matters and show the result, not the spec sheet
Say who should NOT buy it
novelty: A blind test or a long-term follow-up
Compare against a surprising alternative (the cheap option, the DIY option)
detail: Disclose sponsorships and affiliate links
Show prices with the date they were checked

formats.name: Reaction / stitch / duet
formats.definition: Responding to someone else's video, with their clip shown first or alongside.
examples: Stitching a bad tip and correcting it
Duet reacting to a trend

polish: Only keep the 2-3 seconds of the original you need
Use your own visuals for the answer
insight: Add a correction or a fact, not only a reaction
Show proof
novelty: A recurring 'fact-check' series
Answer with an experiment
detail: Credit the original
Be fair to the original creator

formats.name: Meme / trend audio
formats.definition: A trending sound or meme template applied to the niche.
examples: A trending audio with a niche-specific caption
A meme template about a job

polish: Shoot it properly even if the joke is simple
Match cuts to the audio
insight: Make the joke land only for insiders
Hide a real tip in it
novelty: Use the trend's structure, not its exact copy
Be early, or skip it
detail: Check the audio's licence for business accounts
One joke per video

formats.name: AI image slideshow
formats.definition: Generic AI-generated images with an AI voice, generated in bulk.
examples: "Facts about ancient Rome" with AI stills
Motivational AI slideshow

polish: One consistent art direction, curated frames only
Real voice or carefully directed AI voice
insight: Research one fact per video that is not on the first search page
Cite sources
novelty: Animate the stills with parallax and camera moves
Mix AI images with real archival material
detail: Fix hands, text and artefacts
Label AI imagery where platforms require it

layouts.name: Full frame, single subject
layouts.definition: One subject fills the frame; the default vertical shot.

layouts.name: Split screen (top/bottom)
layouts.definition: Two clips stacked, often with unrelated gameplay or satisfying footage below.

layouts.name: Caption-heavy centre text
layouts.definition: Big auto-captions in the middle carry the video.

layouts.name: Picture-in-picture face-cam
layouts.definition: Small face-cam over a screen, document or footage.

layouts.name: Editorial frame / headline bar
layouts.definition: Letterboxed video inside a designed frame with a headline and source line, like a news brand.

layouts.name: Top-down desk / overhead
layouts.definition: Overhead camera on a surface: hands, paper, objects.

layouts.name: Full-screen kinetic type
layouts.definition: Animated words fill the screen in sync with the voice.

layouts.name: Documentary (lower thirds, archive)
layouts.definition: Interviews and archive with lower-third names and dates.

layouts.name: Glass UI / clean interface
layouts.definition: Frosted glass panels, soft shadows and smooth UI motion, in an Apple-like style.

layouts.name: Paper collage
layouts.definition: Halftone cut-outs, paper textures, paint blocks and hand-drawn notes.

layouts.name: Paper → Glass (two acts)
layouts.definition: The problem in rough paper collage, the solution in clean glass UI; the style change is the turn of the story.
